This workspace runs a recruiting desk: employer clients and their fee terms, every open job order, candidates and where each one stands, every submittal from first send to placement, and the fee and guarantee that follow. Your job boards and email stay where they are; this is where the desk sees every search at once.

text.text: Spend your sourcing hours on hot roles first.
Ask for exclusivity for two to three weeks in return for a shortlist by a fixed date. Tick

The maintenance planner role at Arclight is exclusive with a 25 percent fee. The manager wants the planned maintenance software, a scheduling record and clean reports, so the recruiter screens on those three before anything else.
If the pay budget is far below what the must-haves cost in your market, say so with numbers from recent placements. Taking a role you cannot fill costs you time and the client's trust.
Every candidate you send says something about your judgment. Fewer, better submittals win more placements than a stack of résumés.

Do not send a résumé to a company that has not asked for it, and never send a candidate to a client without their consent for that client. Both damage trust on both sides, and in many places they start fee disputes.
Each month, compare submittals with interviews for each recruiter. If fewer than one in three submittals gets an interview, screening needs tightening.

Tobias was submitted for the billing analyst role three days ago with no answer yet. The recruiter calls the hiring manager, learns he is out until Thursday, and tells Tobias so he does not accept another offer by mistake.
The offer stage is where most placements are lost, and the guarantee period is where most fees are refunded. Both need a firm routine.
Ask the candidate for the lowest offer they would accept, and what else they are waiting on.
Ask the client for the offer they plan to make before they make it.
Close the gap before the written offer goes out, not after.
Prepare the candidate for a counter-offer from their current employer. Most counter-offers do not keep people for long; talk about why they wanted to move.
Once accepted in writing, set the start date.

text.text: When one number drops, it shows where to work: sourcing, screening, interview prep or offer handling.
A job order past its target date without an offer gets a straight conversation with the client: change the pay, widen the must-haves, or pause the search.
Look at expected fees on hot roles, fees invoiced and not paid, and placements still in guarantee. Fees in guarantee are not safe until the guarantee passes.

The welding lead role is past its target with one interview this week. The desk agrees to ask Arclight to consider strong welders who have led smaller crews, and Anders gets interview prep on blueprint reading.
Say what is really happening. A role marked hot with no candidates in play for two weeks is not hot; change it. The review only works when the board matches reality.
Each recruiter writes their next steps on the job orders the same day, so the plan lives in the workspace and not in someone's notebook.
